by a sequence of random partitions $\{\mathcal{P}_n\}$ of the natural numbers. At each step $n$, the process selects the next integer $n+1$ to extend the partition by attaching it to an existing element $k \in \mathbb{N}$ with a probability proportional to a "attractiveness" weight $V_k$. This mechanism creates a preferential attachment structure, where frequently selected integers accumulate higher weights and become even more likely to be chosen in the future. We investigate the asymptotic distribution of these partitions, deriving Borel-Titchmarsh-L\'evy measures that characterize their scaling limits. These measures are identified through a zero measure graph representation, which functions as a graphon. Furthermore, we apply these findings to a simplified evolutionary game theory model involving two species, analyzing the large-time asymptotics of the resulting genetic composition. Finally, we examine examples utilizing attractiveness measures that are log concave or log convex. A specific instance involves attractiveness proportional to the $q$-analog of the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{q}$. When $q=1$, the process reduces to the Borel partition process, while $q=\infty$ yields a partitioning variant of the Chinese Restaurant Process. We also explore cases where the attractiveness measure belongs to the one-parameter Poisson-Dirichlet family. Computer simulations illustrate the asymptotic distributions for various values of $q$. This work was conducted as a collaboration between the second and third authors. Keywords: asymptotics, evolutionary game theory, log concavity, log convexity, one-parameter Poisson-Dirichlet measure, preferential attachment, zero measure graph, graphon. a difference-in-means requires estimating the mean outcome under treatment for the control group and the mean outcome under control for the treatment group. While the literature extensively addresses how to measure the outcome under treatment, there is less consensus on how to estimate the outcome under control. This paper argues that OLS provides the optimal estimate of the outcome under control. Consequently, when calculating the ATE, observations in the treatment group should have their control outcomes predicted via OLS, and when observing the ATE in practice, the observed outcome in the treatment group should be adjusted by the difference between the actual mean and the OLS-predicted mean. I validate this approach using a simple simulation and applying it to two datasets: one examining the impact of a job training program on earnings and another analyzing the effect of a policy on teen pregnancy. I also provide a theoretical proof supporting these findings. Concludingly, I demonstrate that OLS is the optimal method for estimating the outcome under control, making this approach applicable in various contexts, including experiments. Specifically, I show that the "intention-to-treat" estimator used in experiments is essentially an OLS estimator. Therefore, experiments can directly utilize the ATE as the estimate of the outcome under control, whereas non-experimental studies must estimate the outcome under treatment and compare it to the OLS-predicted outcome under control. This solution offers a straightforward framework for determining counterfactual outcomes across both experimental and non-experimental settings.

fundamental model for mid-latitude rotating turbulent flows. In this setup, the inner and outer cylindrical walls are maintained at distinct temperatures while the fluid between them rotates as a solid body. We conducted numerical simulations of this system using a spectral method, which offers the benefit of generating time series with high signal-to-noise ratios. Our analysis focused on the auto- and cross-correlation functions for temperature and velocity within turbulent regimes at high Rayleigh numbers. We observed that both auto- and cross-correlation functions display power-law decay across the majority of the time lag range. By applying a nonlinear least-squares fit, we determined the exponents for these correlations, finding that they vary with the Rayleigh number. Additionally, we examined these correlations across the spectral domain, noting that the wavevector spectrum also follows a power law with an exponent that is Rayleigh-number dependent. These numerical findings are compared against existing experimental data and theoretical models. The results suggest that the system's dynamics can be described as an energy exchange between zonal (meridional) flow and turbulent eddies, where eddy self-organization leads to an increase in zonal flow intensity. Specifically, we found that eddies aligned with the most intense turbulent waves exhibit the longest lifetime. Furthermore, the zonal flow acts as a filter that amplifies long-lived, highly organized eddies. These organized eddies continuously transfer energy to the zonal flow, creating a feedback loop where the resulting increase in zonal flow intensity generates new long-lived eddies. This cycle repeats continuously, driving the system toward stronger organization. Finally, we propose a simplified model to interpret our numerical results. This model employs a two-state approach, where the long-living eddies correspond to the state possessing the lowest free energy. We demonstrate that the fitted parameters align with our numerical findings, and we outline the theoretical basis for the model along with its experimental testability. We also provide a brief discussion of other proposed multi-state models. Overall, our study reveals that eddy self-organization generates increasingly intense zonal flows, a phenomenon that has been the subject of extensive debate within experimental geophysical fluid dynamics. While both experiments and simulations confirm the existence of these intense zonal flows, current theoretical explanations remain inadequate. Consequently, there is a critical need for new theoretical frameworks to elucidate the mechanisms behind eddy self-organization and the subsequent intensification of zonal flows. This work aims to contribute to this essential body of theory. **Keywords:** eddy self-organization, zonal

This study examines the light-driven AMM developed by F. Le Doux and J. A. Switzer [J. Phys. Chem. C \textbf{124}, 11007 (2020)], for which only limited experimental data currently exist. $$ (\text{f} \ast_g \text{h})(\text{x}) = \int_{\Omega} \text{f}(\omega) \text{g}(\omega,\text{x}) \text{h}(\varphi(\omega,\text{x})) \text{d}\Omega(\omega), \quad \forall \text{x} \in \text{X}, $$

first T-dwarf, GJ 229B has been the subject of nearly three decades of research into its atmospheric composition and thermal structure. This study utilizes a model discrimination technique applied to new Lick Observatory infrared spectra to evaluate existing atmospheric models against the latest observational data, distinguishing the method from traditional chi-squared analyses that rely on a single best-fit value. By applying this approach to 127 previously published spectra ranging from 0.4 to 5.0 microns, we reject all prior atmospheric models with greater than 99% confidence. We subsequently present a set of models that simultaneously satisfy all constraints, highlighting their primary distinctions. Our results indicate that the previous structure of the deep atmosphere remains largely intact, though the transition zone between the deep and radiative regions is significantly deeper than previously thought. Furthermore, the new data suggest a cooler upper atmosphere, a finding corroborated by the recent detection of methanol. These implications for the planet's thermal structure and chemistry are discussed in relation to recent direct imaging studies of ultra-cool brown dwarfs. Finally, we examine whether this represents the first revised model of an old, field brown dwarf, arguing instead that it is the first of many such revisions, a necessary step in the evolution of atmospheric modeling as observational data improve. The rejection of old models may inadvertently accelerate the adoption of new ones, rather than implying they were incorrect. This study developed a novel computational model to simulate both the aerosol transport process and the resulting infection chain within a classroom setting. The study aimed to investigate how ventilation rates, air mixing intensity, human activities, and infectious doses impact infection transmission. The transmission dynamics were modeled using a SEIR framework, while aerosol transport was analyzed through a Lagrangian particle approach. Simulations were conducted in a standard classroom environment, tracking the concentration of infectious particles in aerosols exhaled by humans and the potential for transmission between students. The integration of this aerosol transport model with the SEIR framework allowed for a detailed examination of infection propagation under varying ventilation conditions and classroom activity levels. The interaction between these models was established such that the particle flux into the lungs of infected persons drives the transition from the exposed to the infectious state, whereas the removal of particles from the room air due to ventilation or mixing processes influences the concentration available for transmission to susceptible persons. This paper outlines the formulation of both the SEIR and particle transport models and presents simulation results for various scenarios. These results demonstrate that the interaction between the particle model and SEIR framework can effectively capture both short-term and long-term dynamics of aerosol transmission. Furthermore, the particle model provided insights into the mechanisms of transmission, showing that a high recirculation fraction combined with poor mixing can delay the concentration rise in the classroom, creating an illusion of safety despite a high particle flux into susceptible lungs. The reported tool is anticipated to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and engineers working in building physics and infectious disease control. A supplementary document contains additional details regarding the model and simulation outcomes. Various sensitivity analyses were performed to assess how transmission is affected by changes in model parameters. Finally, a comparison with a room model that neglects particle removal from the air due to mixing or ventilation is presented. These analyses confirm that the model can capture the essential features of aerosol transmission. Furthermore, the model exhibits a robust response to changes in its parameters. This robustness indicates that, despite uncertainties in specific parameter values, the model remains suitable for quantifying transmission and evaluating mitigation strategies. The model is accessible via an open-source repository at https://github.com/soehne/aerosol_seir.

We examine six relevant nuclear systems: $^{76}$Se, $^{82}$Se, $^{130}$Te, $^{136}$Xe, $^{130}$I, and $^{136}$Cs. By incorporating both single-particle weak matrix elements and configuration mixing, we achieve highly accurate half-life predictions. Our results indicate that including configuration mixing typically reduces predicted half-lives by approximately 10%, though exceptions exist, such as in $^{76}$Se where no significant change occurs, and $^{130}$I and $^{136}$Cs where the effect is negligible. We achieve agreement with experimental data within uncertainties for six out of the seven cases. The only discrepancy arises for $^{82}$Se, where our predicted half-life deviates from measurements by more than $2\sigma$. Our findings suggest that the current shell-model approach, utilizing a modified Groshart et al. single-particle parameter set and a balanced balanced interaction, offers a reliable and accurate method for computing nuclear weak transition matrix elements. Furthermore, we observe that next-to-next-to-next-to-halo orbitals (N$^{3}$H) play a critical role in this decay process. Finally, we provide an open-source code for weak transition calculations, available at \url{https://github.com/WeiQianLi/wm_weak}. This code can be readily adapted for other beta-decay processes, including two-neutrino double $\beta$-decay, neutrinoless double $\beta$-decay, inverse $\beta$-decay, neutrino capture, and $\alpha$-decay. A detailed user manual, also accessible at the same repository, accompanies the code. Our tools are designed to facilitate the analysis of weak nuclear processes using future high-accuracy ab initio or next-generation interaction-to-fidelity shell-model interactions. These findings will be particularly valuable for the next generation of double $\beta$-decay experiments. Published in Physical Review C, 105, 014310 (2022).

This study examines the accuracy of state estimation within double-sided auctions driven by Poisson arrival times, with a specific focus on inference errors regarding an unseen order book. By employing a hidden Markov model to represent the process, we analyze estimation accuracy using the Kalman-Bucy filter and the extended Kalman filter. Our numerical findings indicate that the estimation error of the player's strategy process grows over time in the Poisson auction setting when utilizing the Kalman-Bucy filter. Furthermore, we assess the performance of both filters in a market environment where double-sided auctions follow a non-homogeneous Poisson process, finding that the extended Kalman filter yields significantly more accurate estimates than its homogeneous Poisson counterpart. These parameters are interpreted through the lens of the Accretion Induced Collapse (AIC) of white dwarfs (WDs) within binary star systems, aiming to elucidate the evolution of MSP binaries. Our results indicate that the majority of WD-MSP binaries consist of WDs with masses exceeding 1.0 solar masses and spin periods exceeding 1 day. We demonstrate that a substantial fraction of AIC events occur in close binary systems, where the proto-neutron star is spun up by the donor WD. The observed distribution of WD spin periods supports this scenario, as significant angular momentum transfer via tidal forces in close binaries accelerates the WD. Furthermore, we show that tidal interaction transfers both linear and angular momentum from the WD to the proto-neutron star, resulting in much longer spin periods for the newly born MSP. Additionally, most donor WDs in our sample possess radii larger than their zero temperature values, indicating recent contraction following the cessation of cooling. The timescale for this contraction is approximately equal to the spin period, as predicted by standard stellar evolution models. This mechanism ensures that the donor WD remains in a quasi-steady state before initiating accretion onto the MSP. The mass accretion rate during the accretion phase is estimated at $\sim 10^{-10} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$. The accumulation of angular momentum and mass during this phase further spins up the proto-neutron star. The interplay between angular momentum accumulation and mass accretion explains the high mass and ultra-long spin periods of MSPs. We conclude that our model aligns with current observational data, suggesting that AIC in binary systems represents a viable formation channel for MSPs with extremely long spin periods. During the accretion phase, the radiative luminosity is approximately $10^{38}$ erg/s, which is sufficient to produce X-ray binaries. Finally, we show that the luminosity from the cooling of the newly born MSP is negligible compared to that of a typical neutron star formed in a supernova explosion. transiting gas giant with a highly eccentric orbit, experiences dramatic and rapid variations in stellar irradiation during its periastron passage. This unique environment has made it an ideal subject for atmospheric studies using phase-curve observations. However, current theoretical models struggle to explain the system's photometric data. To address this discrepancy, we introduce a theoretical framework based on the coupling between magnetohydrodynamics and radiative transfer. Our model incorporates key features of eccentric orbital systems, such as atmospheric expansion and a prolonged periastron approach, alongside specific characteristics of HD 80606b, including atmospheric magnetization and periastron heating. We applied this model to recent phase curve observations from the Wide-field Camera 3 on the Hubble Space Telescope, as well as prior transit and secondary eclipse data. The results reveal that the observed day-night temperature contrast is primarily driven by the combined effects of radiative cooling and slow radiative transfer within the upper atmosphere. Additionally, we detected a weak but distinct eccentricity signal in the day-side temperature, which is best accounted for by radiative heating combined with slow radiative transfer. These findings offer new insights into the physics governing gas giant responses to varying stellar flux and suggest this approach may be broadly applicable to future atmospheric studies of eccentric gas giants. However, the persistent mismatch between theory and observation for HD 80606b underscores the need for more sensitive atmospheric measurements. Such data could reveal new physical phenomena, such as non-equilibrium chemistry or cloud formation, that are essential for accurately modeling the system. These measurements are anticipated from the James Webb Space Telescope. By comparing HD 80606b to other eccentric gas giants observed by JWST, we can better distinguish between atmospheric physics and cloud effects. This study demonstrates the utility of a magnetohydrodynamics-radiative transfer coupled model for predicting gas giant responses to eccentric orbits, which is critical for interpreting atmospheric observations of eccentric gas giants around target stars in the HD 80606b system. These observations aim to clarify the physical mechanisms behind the system's anomalous signal. Furthermore, our approach provides a robust method for modeling the responses of gas giants to eccentric stellar irradiation, a phenomenon expected to be prevalent in a significant fraction of exoplanetary systems. Finally, we highlight that the methods employed are broadly applicable to modeling the coupled interaction between a stellar wind and a planetary atmosphere. state has been debated for decades. Although it was traditionally viewed as a compact, spatially localized configuration of six alpha particles, a model-independent analysis of the $6\alpha$ channel using the properties of the collective exciton state $0^+_2$ now indicates that the state may possess significant spatially extended, non-interacting three-$\alpha$-particle correlations. This study examines the role of such spatially extended, non-interacting three-body correlations in alpha-particle-rich exotic nuclei using the exciton model.

**Method:** The collective exciton state $0^+_2$ in $^{12}$C, which lies 1.8 MeV below the three-body threshold, serves as a benchmark. To assess the impact of non-interacting three-body correlations, we calculate the particle number fluctuations below the $0^+_2$ state by comparing results from the fully correlated exciton model (FCEM) with those from the mean-field correlated exciton model (MCEM). The latter is a generalization of the widely used correlated Gaussian model (CGC) that explicitly incorporates particle interactions. FCEM and MCEM correspond to the limits of zero and infinite exciton motion, respectively. To evaluate particle number fluctuations below the $0^+_2$ state, we apply both FCEM and MCEM to the $\gamma$-resonance region in $^{12}$C and analyze the nuclear equation of state (EoS) for isospin asymmetric nuclear matter using the same models.

**Results:** Below the $0^+_2$ state, the MCEM-predicted particle number fluctuations are 20% lower than those predicted by FCEM. This difference stems from the fact that MCEM accounts for short-range correlations, which reduce the probability of non-interacting three-body correlations. Consequently, the particle number fluctuations below the $0^+_2$ state align well with the enhanced collective excitation observed in inelastic electron scattering. Regarding EoS calculations, the MCEM results indicate that the compressibility of isospin asymmetric nuclear matter is 10% lower than that produced by FCEM. This finding suggests that spatially extended, non-interacting three-body correlations have a minor impact on the compressibility of isospin asymmetric nuclear matter.

Go is a two-player game characterized by simple rules, a vast state space, and high depth. Players take turns placing black and white stones on an infinite grid; however, a player loses if they cannot make a move. Each stone connects orthogonally to others of the same color, forming groups. Adjacent groups of opposite colors are considered enemies. The objective is to control more territory than the opponent. The game concludes when both players agree no further moves will benefit either side. Scoring involves counting the territory controlled by the black player, which includes points on the board plus two additional points for each white stone the white player has placed. While players can pass without points, doing so is generally suboptimal.

The board is represented as a 19x19 grid where each cell holds a stone of a specific color. The game begins with an empty board. A move consists of placing a black or white stone on an unoccupied cell. Stones placed on the board remain fixed. A group is defined as a set of connected stones of the same color; connectivity occurs orthogonally between adjacent positions. Groups of opposite colors located adjacently are classified as enemy groups.

Territory refers to empty points surrounded entirely by stones of a single color. Black's score is calculated by summing the points of all empty points that constitute Black's territory. White's score is determined by taking the total points of White's territory and adding two points for every white stone currently on the board.

The move history is represented as a sequence of positions, where each position is a 19x19 grid indicating the state of the board at that moment. The black player moves first, followed by the white player, and this turn-based sequence continues. The game ends when both players pass consecutively. At termination, the score is computed by adding the points of all white stones on the board to the territory points controlled by Black.

Abstract: Deploying Machine Learning often faces significant challenges, such as dealing with opaque black-box models, lacking uncertainty estimates, and facing issues with incomplete data. Additionally, missing values present further complexities. This work tackles these problems by utilizing missing data to estimate uncertainty and by implementing techniques to interpret Machine Learning models. Our findings indicate that while no single estimator is universally superior, specific estimators outperform others on certain datasets. We end by outlining potential future research paths.

Task alignment is a core component of sequence labeling, yet it remains underexplored due to its computational difficulty. ### Introduction

As practical courses in software testing evolve to mirror the demands of the industry, researchers have developed various tools to help students meet code coverage requirements. These initiatives reflect a growing recognition that novice testers face significant challenges when confronting the scale and complexity of large codebases. Specifically, determining which parts of the code to test is a complex task that often exceeds the capabilities of beginners. This difficulty stems from the vast number of lines a student must examine to reach the target under consideration. Consequently, lines that remain untested often result from two issues: (1) the line was simply overlooked, or (2) the line was intentionally placed out of the student's path to ensure specific coverage was not achieved. Distinguishing between these two scenarios is complex and can be frustrating for students.

This approach mirrors real-world software development teams, where developers assist each other in understanding code that is new to them. By adopting this peer-assisted strategy, students engage in valuable learning about how teams collaborate to acquire necessary knowledge. We examine spatially curved cosmological solutions within specific $\alpha$-attractor models that incorporate non-minimal kinetic couplings and non-trivial potential couplings. Our analysis reveals that the asymptotic anti-de Sitter (AdS) de Sitter (dS) scaling solution is generally unstable to entropy perturbations, with the degree of instability inversely proportional to the e-folding number. Consequently, these models may require substantial e-folding numbers, suggesting that kinetic couplings play a pivotal role in the inflationary epoch. Furthermore, we investigate the AdS dS transition and associated particle production in these frameworks. Our findings indicate that under typical conditions, these models fail to support a smooth transition from AdS to dS, resulting in either no particle production or excessive generation. Finally, we identify specific conditions under which a smooth AdS-dS transition occurs, noting that this scenario yields significant particle production. These outcomes offer fresh insights for connecting $\alpha$-attractor models of inflation with reheating mechanisms, such as preheating. Additionally, the stability of entropy perturbations imposes constraints on the e-folding number, necessitating further research into models with large e-folding numbers for potential future observational confirmation.

Recently, it has been suggested that vector inflation could occur during the reheating phase, offering a mechanism for nonthermal dark matter generation. In this study, we analyze scalar perturbations arising from a curvature vector coupling in such scenarios. We determine the constraints on dark matter abundance imposed by these scalar perturbations and their alignment with cosmic microwave background data. We also explore the effects of vector nonlinearity on these findings. Our results indicate that these constraints are robust, even when accounting for vector nonlinearity, and can be relaxed if specific parameters are sufficiently small. We conclude that cosmological vector inflation remains a viable candidate for dark matter production. Additionally, we highlight that these models offer a fresh perspective on the origin of vector fields and can be tested through future investigations into vector dark matter.

Following the determination of the Higgs boson mass, the Higgs self-coupling has emerged as the most critical parameter for future collider experiments. This is because the shape of the inflationary potential is closely linked to the Higgs self-interaction. In this work, we investigate whether a consistent theory can exist that accommodates both a Higgs self-coupling compatible with observed inflationary data and a stable electroweak vacuum.

While automated noise reduction and virtual stethoscope (VS) technologies have shown promise in previous research, no prior study has addressed both areas simultaneously. This paper introduces a deep learning-based denoising VS (DL-BNVS) framework that leverages sub-bands extracted via a Gaussian Model (GM) and a Perceptual Model (PM) to enhance noise reduction across diverse heart sounds. Our results indicate that the DL-BNVS approach yields superior noise reduction performance compared to a baseline solution utilizing a Gaussian Model (DL-GMVB) across all VS positions. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of our proposed DL-GMVB method with ten existing state-of-the-art denoising techniques across four VS positions. Our findings demonstrate that DL-GMVB outperforms the best existing method by at least 10% in terms of SNR across all VS positions. Ultimately, the DL-BNVS framework offers a novel, automated, and efficient solution for enhancing noise reduction in VS acoustic data to support downstream heart sound analysis. Mathematics and Statistics has offered an honors course titled "The Four Colors of Theorem," which examines four distinct theorems across various domains of mathematics. Last semester, students examined color theory within graph theory, the Zeckendorf theorem concerning Fibonacci numbers and base phi, the Borsuk-Ulanovsky theorem on topology and dimensionality, and the Cartan-Akizuki theorem regarding commutative algebra. Last fall, this course was adapted for middle school students as "The Four Colors of Story," designed to illustrate how renowned mathematicians have employed narrative to elucidate complex concepts. In this narrative-driven course, middle school students explored the history of mathematics through the lives and works of four key figures: Euclid, Al-Khwarizmi, Proclus, and Galileo. The curriculum included an examination of the Elements, the origins of algebra, the pedagogical use of parables in religious contexts, and the relationship between science and storytelling. To bring these ideas to life, we presented "Mathematical Tales," where we performed original stories that wove together the authors' biographies, their intellectual contributions, and the narrative power inherent in mathematics. This course was delivered through lectures, discussions, and creative writing exercises. Last fall, middle school students discovered that mathematics is not merely a collection of cold, abstract formulas, but a vibrant field rich with human passion, emotion, and the profound utility of story.

The novel approach to addressing these issues involves a nonlocal framework for cosmic acceleration that resolves the Hubble tension. In this model, the Hubble parameter is expressed as $H(z) = H_0\left[\frac{(1+z)^{q}}{1+\frac{z(2+ z) q}{z_T}}\right]$, where $z_T$ represents the Irwin depth (a parameter with astrophysical significance) and $q$ is a free parameter. This formulation yields an effective equation of state given by $w(z) = \frac{2(1-\Omega_m(z))}{3[1-(1+E_k(z))\frac{z(2+ z) q}{z_T}]}- \frac{1}{1+\frac{z(2+ z) q}{z_T}}$, where $E_k(z) = \frac{z(1+z) q^2}{z_T}$. The framework resolves the Hubble tension by incorporating a cutoff in high-redshift expansion, thereby supporting $H_0 = 73.8^{+0.6}_{-0.8}$ km/s/Mpc, which aligns with Planck 2018 observations under the $\Lambda$CDM assumption. Additionally, setting $w(z) = w_0$ leads to $w_0 = -1 + \frac{2 q^2}{z_T} - \frac{1}{z_T} - \frac{q^2}{z_T(2 z +2)}$, a relationship that correlates the Irwin depth with the sign of the cosmological constant. Analysis of the equation of state, deceleration parameter, and other state variables reveals the nature of cosmic acceleration. Results indicate that $z_T \sim 10^{10} h^{-1}$ Mpc, a value consistent with the age of the universe. Furthermore, the Irwin depth is found to be independent of the Hubble parameter and the assumption of spatial flatness. By applying this model to supernova data, we conclude that the IqCDM framework is viable. Finally, we examine the implications of this theory for black hole entropy and the universe's total energy. We present algorithms for constructing bases of local admissible orders on free modules and determine the local Gröbner sets of module ideals associated with coherent families of ideals. While the free module Gröbner theory for polynomial rings relies on commutative algebra methods, particularly Hilbert-Samuel polynomials, the development of free module Gröbner theory for local Noetherian rings is largely algorithmic. Consequently, the Hilbert-Samuel polynomials of such rings can be freely determined. Furthermore, the results presented here can be extended to other algebraic structures, such as affine monoid algebras and power series rings. These findings may assist in advancing the free module Gröbner theory for other algebraic structures built upon local Noetherian rings. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in instruction following, yet they frequently generate hallucinated details when specific context is absent. While recent studies have addressed this by prompting models to retrieve answers from provided text, there remains a lack of research on how to effectively rank multiple retrieved documents to ensure the model accesses the most relevant information. To address this gap, we propose a novel approach where the model conditionally attends to a single selected document during answer generation. We implement this using a lightweight sequential ranking network that selects one document from those retrieved by a dense vector encoder. Experiments on two multi-hop question answering datasets show that our method outperforms strong baselines, achieving state-of-the-art results on HotpotQA and obtaining competitive BEER scores on Complex-WebQuestions. Our source code is available at https://github.com/parshasr/conditional-attention. Our results have been accepted for publication at CLEVR 2021.

This study introduces the initial formulation of quantum solar entropy, building upon prior work on quantum Von Neumann entropy and quantum entropy derived from Wigner functions. We further establish a complete relationship between these variants of quantum solar entropy and thermodynamic entropy, thereby providing a rigorous informational framework for thermodynamics that extends both classical and prior quantum entropy models. Consequently, this work elucidates the thermodynamic significance of various forms of solar entropy and ultimately demonstrates that Shannon entropy constitutes a lower bound for thermodynamic entropy. The final section illustrates the practical application of this framework through a simplified yet representative system: a two-level atom interacting with a single-mode electromagnetic field. Our findings indicate that the quantum solar entropy of the atom and field individually does not consistently converge to the classical limit. Furthermore, we show that while classical entropy remains invariant under unitary time evolution, the quantum entropy of the system can fluctuate. We conclude that the model system exhibits positive quantum solar entropy, which aligns with the thermodynamic entropy of the atomic system as previously established. Finally, we demonstrate that both Naimpally's and our observations regarding positive solar entropy in thermodynamic systems corroborate the classical result: random processes possess higher entropy than regular ones. These insights offer valuable context for emerging quantum technologies, including quantum information processing, quantum communication, and quantum thermodynamics. Furthermore, this research contributes to fundamental physics by revealing that solar entropy provides an upper bound for the quantum entanglement between interacting systems in a Markovian environment. We also establish the link between Von Neumann and solar entropy and prove that entanglement is maximized when the sum of solar entropies of the components equals zero. This extends Entropia's observation that two-level systems interacting with a Markovian field possess negative solar entropy. Ultimately, we illustrate that entropy can serve as a measure of correlation, and we show that entanglement reaches its maximum when thermodynamic entropy attains its minimum. This study not only clarifies the quantum nature of solar entropy but also offers new theoretical foundations for entropy-based measures of quantum resources. Additionally, it establishes an explicit lower bound on solar entropy for physical states and offers an operational interpretation for negative solar entropy. We demonstrate that states with negative solar entropy can be converted into thermal states, and that thermal states can be transformed into states with reduced energy. Federated learning (FL) addresses this by training deep neural networks across distributed data without centralizing it, offering a promising path to balancing scalability with privacy. However, the risk of inferring training data from the trained model remains, as FL still lacks robust privacy guarantees. This is particularly critical for deep neural networks, which often overfit to their training data. Consequently, researchers are exploring the use of FAIR (obfuscated yet accurate) models, which are intentionally overfitted to create performance traps that prevent overtraining. These traps serve as a form of watermarking, deterring model extraction by malicious actors who might reuse the model for inference instead of just stealing it. By treating FL as a competitive game between a provider and potential thieves, we introduce a federated deep learning game (FLG) framework. In this framework, we apply federated obfuscation (FO) techniques to develop a Federated Obfuscation Game (FOG) with deep neural network performance traps. Our results demonstrate that FO successfully integrates deep learning into the FL framework, and through extensive experiments, we show that FOG can achieve FAIR models while maintaining competitive performance against traditional centralized learning and standard federated learning approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/iamdavidwu/Federated-Obfuscation.

, yet their "black box" nature hinders their adoption in high-stakes fields like medicine and law. To address this opacity, researchers have turned to the interpretation of data-driven models. While numerous techniques and metrics exist to assess interpretability, their comparative performance has not been thoroughly evaluated. Consequently, their utility as standards within the interpretation community remains uncertain. Our study aims to resolve this gap by systematically analyzing a dataset of 1,000 cases from the Opinions dataset. We compare existing metrics for supervised classification using various supervised learning models trained on different feature subsets. We conclude that no single metric universally outperforms others in predicting case outcomes. This result underscores the necessity of a supervised learning approach that moves beyond simple feature selection toward a more nuanced feature weighting system. Such a system would enable models to generate plausibility scores for individual features, facilitating a shift from a binary classification mindset to one that acknowledges and utilizes varying degrees of relevance. This paper represents the first step toward developing this generalized, interpretable weighted machine learning system. Furthermore, we propose a set of research questions and directions to guide future work and the field of interpretation generally. We believe these inquiries will inspire a broader understanding of how supervised models utilize features and how that utilization can be measured and predicted. Finally, we outline our ongoing project, which seeks to instantiate these questions through a prototype. This prototype employs natural language features and established classification algorithms to forecast whether US Supreme Court justices will rule for the plaintiff or defendant in case classification tasks. By demonstrating that no interpretation metric currently exists that predicts algorithm behavior more accurately than the features themselves, our work seeks to inspire a new generation of models and interpretation metrics. We posit that the interpretation community must move away from treating interpretation as a series of post-hoc explanations for opaque models and instead focus on designing more transparent models from the outset. We present our findings at the Conference on AI and Law (2020). The source code is available at https://github.com/alecstef/Opinions-features.

In many nations, including the US, China, and South Korea, artificial intelligence (AI) development is driven by large-scale, high-performance computing centers. Conversely, Canada lacks a national AI supercomputing facility, with only two research groups gaining intermittent access to external national resources. This paper presents the case for developing a dedicated national AI supercomputing center in Canada, accompanied by an initial proposal for such a facility. We outline the benefits of centralized resource management and present rough estimates for anticipated returns on investment and the underinvestment caused by the current fragmented and limited access to national AI computing infrastructure. We also address potential locations and size considerations, alongside an assessment of implementation challenges and timelines. Finally, we propose next steps for advancing this initiative. Building on a preliminary discussion at the Canadian AI and Big Data Summit in November 2019, we encourage the AI community to engage with this proposal and explore ways to refine and adopt it.

On November 11, 2019, the Canadian government announced a $100 million contribution toward a proposed national AI supercomputing center, known as the Institute of AI and Advanced Integration (A3IAI), to be hosted at the University of Waterloo. This decision comes nearly a decade after Canada's initial failed attempt to establish a national AI supercomputing center. Although the involvement of the government validates the necessity and strategic importance of such an institute, it does not resolve the specific challenges regarding location, scale, implementation timeline, and lead organization. However, this plan falls significantly short of China's current AI supercomputing capacity and is roughly half the size of the US National AI Research Center. der$ and $Wilson$ algorithms are prominent methods for generating uniform spanning trees (USTs). Through numerical simulations, we analyze their scattering and energy dynamics. The results indicate that for parameters with a "strong" IDDS effect, both the number of small-amplitude 22-dimensional (22D) bound states matching the initial data's symmetry and their retained dispersion dispersion energy increase. Conversely, "weak" IDDS yields no symmetric bound states, and the dispersion energy is nearly identical across different parameter sets. We attribute these outcomes to the competition between attractive and repulsive forces in the IDDS term. Furthermore, the intensity of the initial condition determines the relative strength of these forces. These findings offer theoretical support for the design of soliton arrays in diverse applications. Additionally, we demonstrate that the IGS method, combined with a novel conservation law, achieves optimal spectral accuracy in space with high computational efficiency. Extensive 2D and 3D simulations confirm these bounds and soliton dynamics, with 2D runs taking 2.5 hours and 3D runs 18.5 hours on a single CPU. In contrast, running the same simulations using the split-step method would require 100+ hours per dimension. These soliton configurations in the NLS with IDDS are theoretically applicable to precision cold atom positioning and the control of chemical reactions. The observations regarding the quantity and quality of bound states in this model hold potential significance for modeling multi-electron atoms and molecules. Finally, we note that similar phenomena are expected to occur in other models featuring intensity-dependent coefficients. (This article is part of a special issue dedicated to David Keating).

This category encompasses oriented submersions, orientation-preserving local diffeomorphisms, and radial projections centered at fixed points as specific instances. The paper further explores the properties of these maps, with a primary focus on how they influence the homotopy types of the involved manifolds. In this context, we establish a stochastic version of the Whitehead Theorem. Additionally, we provide a new demonstration of the Levi-Civita method for desuspending spheres via one-point compactification. These findings imply that for any manifold $M$ with a non-empty boundary, the inclusion of the one-point compactification of the interior into the one-point compactification of $M$ induces an isomorphism on the homotopy groups of $M$. Finally, we propose several open questions and conjectures regarding oriented colored broken submersions. Notably, we suggest a conjecture that would serve as an "inverse" sub-sphere transfer theorem. However, we also highlight that counterexamples exist, as a specific variant of the Lebesgue Transfer Theorem can fail for such maps. Such counterexamples yield new examples of homotopy equivalent compact, connected, closed manifolds that are not diffeomorphic yet share the same one-point compactification. Consequently, this raises the inquiry of constructing such a broken submersion between manifolds with distinct one-point compactifications. While this remains an open problem, we do present an example of a map resembling a broken submersion—specifically, the suspension of a submersion between non-compact manifolds—that achieves this result. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the suspension of a submersion between compact manifolds does indeed induce an isomorphism on the homotopy groups of the targets. These counterexamples stem from the Levine-Ravenel Theorem, which we utilize to calculate the rational homotopy groups of certain projective varieties. This leads to an explicit description of the homotopy groups for a broad class of complete non-compact Kähler manifolds. As a corollary, we provide a positive answer to a question posed by Dugger and Isaksen in [DuggerIsaksen14]. We also discuss an alternative approach to deriving Levine-Ravenel Theorems using the properties of oriented colored broken submersions. The primary objective is to assess how effectively these methods scale with increasing mesh refinement and parallelize across multi-domain setups. Using ABAQUS/Standard, we analyzed the deformation of a soft, hyperelastic, and nearly incompressible rectangular block subjected to uniaxial compression. We focused on refining the finite element mesh within the compression zone and examined the impact of varying BDDC and AMG multigrid tolerance settings on solver performance. This research addresses a gap in the literature, as there is a lack of studies on scalable solvers for cardiovascular simulations, which is essential for the efficient execution of more complex and demanding simulations. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was conducted on the non-linear material parameters of the phantom to demonstrate how solver performance is influenced by the complexity of the problem. Finally, we explored how the number of subdomains in BDDC and the AMG preconditioner configuration affect computational performance. The findings indicate that AMG often complements BDDC well; specifically, BDDC typically precondition an AMG solver to achieve optimal results. This combined approach is particularly advantageous for coarse meshes or scenarios involving high material non-linearity and BDDC subdomain eigenvalue spectra. This work was performed as a Master's thesis at the University of Pittsburgh. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/edwinfrancop/edwinfrancop.

The advent of user-generated content has transformed how individuals access and share information. Platforms like blogs, micro-blogs, and social media have lowered the barriers to entry, enabling the easy publication of updates and pages. Although many personalization and recommendation algorithms exist, they often rely on collaborative filtering, which demands a substantial number of users and items to function effectively. This work focuses on two use cases to illustrate the advantages of the proposed algorithm. The first involves new users or organizations seeking high-quality content; for instance, a new researcher or student looking for scientific papers. The second targets existing users who, despite having customized feeds, still encounter duplicate or less relevant information. In both instances, the algorithm successfully delivers relevant data, even if it differs from what the recipient currently possesses. The core mechanism involves extracting key information from various sources and delivering it to the target. This paper details the algorithm's characteristics and demonstrates its effectiveness through these two applications.

These obstacles stem partly from conventional bianisotropic metamaterial models, which rely on complex multilayer periodic structures, and partly from prior attempts at effective Bianisotropic Periodic Boundary Conditions (Bianisotropic PBCs), which depend heavily on finite-element interpolation and extrapolation of field values across periodic boundaries. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces a novel homogenized bianisotropic PBC that is both physically realizable and mathematically robust. These new conditions are derived from a nonlocal local variational formulation of Maxwell's equations by applying homogenization techniques directly to the boundary layers near periodic interfaces. Consequently, they facilitate the creation of bianisotropic acoustic metamaterials using simple periodic boundary layers while enabling their integration into existing multilayer acoustic meta-devices through effective medium theory. Furthermore, these conditions allow for the formulation of a homogenized transmission matrix (T-matrix) representation for Bianisotropic periodic media (BPMs). This approach bypasses the finite-element interpolation and extrapolation problems inherent in earlier PBC formulations, thereby enabling new effective homogenized meta-devices based on BPMs. To validate these findings, a periodic acoustic barrier constructed from solid rubber layers separated by air gaps was designed, analyzed, and experimentally tested, demonstrating that the proposed homogenized bianisotropic PBC accurately captures the scattering behavior of the physical meta-material. Finally, the paper presents a noise control application utilizing a new effective Bianisotropic periodic media (BPM) multilayer coating, comparing its performance against other current multilayer absorbers. This new meta-material was also tested experimentally, confirming that the proposed homogenized bianisotropic PBC accurately models the scattering of the actual acoustic meta-material. However, the limited capacity of wireless interfaces necessitates careful planning of node placements and network configurations. To address this, we introduce a novel optimization framework that determines optimal network structures, node locations, and resource allocation to maximize total IAB network throughput. This framework accounts for user equipment (UE) demands, power consumption, interference, and the impact of concurrent transmissions on multiple hops. Since the optimization problem is non-convex, we develop a decomposition approach that splits it into two sub-problems: IAB node placement and network configuration. An alternating algorithm is employed to solve these sub-problems iteratively until convergence. For the node placement sub-problem, we design a solution based on the facility location method, while the network configuration sub-problem is resolved using Lagrangian relaxation combined with a branch-and-bound technique for global optimization. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our proposed algorithm significantly outperforms other IAB network structures and placement strategies. Furthermore, we compare IAB nodes with traditional small cells and find that IAB offers higher throughput, UEs achieve greater satisfaction, and the network operates more efficiently. These results indicate that joint optimization of IAB node placement and network configuration enhances IAB performance more effectively than other approaches. Additionally, IAB networks provide superior performance compared to traditional small cell architectures.

The integration of Unlicensed Access Points (WAPs) into next-generation wireless networks aims to increase network capacity and density. However, the non-orthogonal nature of wireless media makes it difficult to guarantee Quality of Service (QoS) for users. To tackle this, we propose a joint optimization framework for location and sub-channel assignment of WAPs, ensuring QoS for all users. We also develop a WAP initialization procedure to start the framework. Due to the problem's NP-hard complexity, we introduce a decomposition approach to address the location and sub-channel assignment issues separately. For sub-channel assignment, we utilize a matching algorithm to maximize user satisfaction, and a heuristic method is applied to solve the location problem. Given that the decomposition algorithm may converge to a local optimum, we also present a centralized approach to find the global optimum for small-scale networks. Simulation results confirm that our proposed methods substantially improve WAP utilization and density. We also compare our decomposition-based solutions with a centralized method for small networks, showing that both approaches yield performance very close to the centralized global optimum. Finally,

We then identify a condition for non-radiation that holds across all inertial frames, a requirement that is intuitively necessary for the stability of atomic systems, and demonstrate its equivalence to specific relations between charge and current, including the wave equation. We consider these findings as a contribution to the convergence of various physical schools thought to be addressing the same fundamental problem from different perspectives. This perspective integrates elements of classical electrodynamics, general relativity, and quantum mechanics. De Broglie-Bohm quantum mechanics is utilized to establish a boundary condition for classical electrodynamics, guiding its development toward a "correct" theory for describing "correct" matter. This "correct" matter is characterized by an acceleration proportional to the gravitational field and possesses a mass identical to the Planck mass. These outcomes could potentially facilitate a unification of these physical disciplines.

This paper introduces a novel hierarchical deep reinforcement learning framework designed for sample-efficient training of control policies in multi-task environments. The proposed system comprises multiple task modules, where each module is modeled as a linear dynamical system with latent states that govern a local non-linear transition function and an observation function. Unlike prior methods, inferring hierarchical states is framed as a multi-task bandit problem, enabling the efficient identification of common sub-tasks. We detail an efficient approximate inference algorithm and demonstrate through extensive experiments on both simulated and real robotic systems that the proposed framework effectively scales to multi-task control problems. These methods serve as the foundational technology for the NASA RoboJove system, which has been deployed on various ground-based experiments. Extensive evaluations on a real mobile robot reveal that the approach achieves a substantial reduction in both sample and computational complexity compared to existing methods. This work establishes a new foundation for training multi-task models using limited data, offering an effective solution for controlling complex non-linear dynamical systems. The code is accessible at https://github.com/amanjain2000/HDL-ZPS.

Current learning-based motion planning approaches typically rely on sampling methods like RRT* to explore a state space defined by an approximate dynamics model. However, these techniques often fail to learn accurate models from limited samples, and their planning phase is generally too slow for high-frequency control applications. This letter proposes a new framework for learning model-predictive control using reinforcement learning, where the underlying dynamics model is represented as a graph with a fixed topology. This structure enables efficient planning by allowing the search for low-cost trajectories to be conducted via graph search. Training the model involves sampling system trajectories and learning a locally linear transition function for each segment. Experimental results on a real differential drive robot indicate that the learned controller can track desired trajectories with an RMS error of 0.08 m at 100 Hz, while achieving a 10x reduction in training time and a 3x reduction in the number of required samples compared to similar state-of-the-art methods. This approach is integral to the RoboJove system, which supports diverse ground exploration missions for NASA research. The code is available at https://github.com/amanjain2000/MGRL.

This process is critical for intent recognition systems to handle unknown inputs and accurately classify them into the correct intent categories. Currently, intent discovery typically relies on supervised machine learning methods, which demand extensive user annotations and extensive training data. Although recent approaches leverage self-supervised or unsupervised generation techniques to extract features or generate data for discovery, these methods necessitate numerous fully annotated examples for each target intent category, rendering the training cost-prohibitive in many practical scenarios. To address this challenge, we introduce UFD (intent discovery via unsupervised contrastive feature learning), which eliminates the need for any annotated examples from the target intent categories while achieving state-of-the-art results. Specifically, UFD utilizes an existing intent taxonomy and a few known user utterances to discover new intent categories. It constructs an unsupervised model trained on unlabeled data, generates pseudo-labeled data, and performs contrastive feature learning to identify different intent categories. Evaluations across six real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. We have open-sourced the code at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-UDCUDS-UFD. We anticipate this approach will offer significant guidance for intent discovery scenarios where rich organizational domain knowledge exists but annotated data for target categories is scarce or absent. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00287.

While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved great success, their reliance on local filters restricts their ability to model long-range spatial relationships effectively. To address this limitation, researchers have increasingly turned to Transformer networks, which utilize self-attention mechanisms to successfully model long-range structure in other domains. This paper introduces the First-In-Order-Attention (FIO-Att) mechanism, a novel self-attention approach designed for early vision representation learning. FIO-Att significantly reduces the quadratic computational complexity of standard multi-head attention while delivering performance that rivals, and in certain cases exceeds, that of recent state-of-the-art scene understanding models. FIO-Att operates on the insight that long-range structure is crucial for vision tasks, yet only the earliest network activations possess the rich, high-level semantic information necessary to leverage it. FIO-Att efficiently captures these long-range dependencies by restricting attention operations to a linear number of sequence tokens based on their temporal order. FIO-Att was evaluated on the Microsoft COCO captioning and detection tasks, as well as the AllenAI Object Detection Benchmark. The results demonstrate that FIO-Att achieves state-of-the-art performance in captioning and detection, as well as in image classification. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinr1999/FIO-Att. Our findings indicate that long-range dependencies are vital for early vision representation learning, and FIO-Att provides an efficient method for modeling them.

This background is most intense at frequencies corresponding to the mass scale of intermediate-scale physics. Within this range, the cosmic spectrum closely mirrors the frequency-dependent emission rate, creating a distinct peak at Hawking frequencies linked to intermediate masses. The amplitude of this peak is roughly three orders of magnitude lower than the cosmological background radiation at frequencies below 1 THz. However, the radiation intensity becomes comparable to the background at terahertz frequencies and at terahertz cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperatures. Consequently, intermediate black hole evaporation radiation may be detectable through future advancements in instrumentation and refined data analysis techniques applied to CMB data. If intermediate-scale physics exists at the TeV scale, the spectrum would lack a peak, and the resulting cosmological radiation would be even less abundant. The text also addresses a scenario where the Hawking radiation frequency is much greater than the expansion rate, which applies to very early intermediate-scale physics or heavy black holes. In this regime, the radiation spectrum redshifts to lower frequencies, and a peak forms at frequencies where the emission rate and redshift factor are balanced. Finally, we explore the potential for detecting this radiation via its interaction with CMB photons. If the Hawking radiation frequency is significantly lower than the CMB temperature, radiation from intermediate black holes could induce measurable changes in the CMB spectrum. Conversely, if the frequency is much higher, the radiation could distort the CMB power spectrum at large angular scales. Detecting such radiation would confirm Hawking radiation and offer valuable insights into the early universe. Furthermore, we examine a scenario where all primordial black holes have evaporated, leaving no black holes to suppress light element abundances during Big Bang nucleosynthesis. In this case, the radiation from intermediate black holes must not exceed the CMB radiation density at the time of light element formation. This constraint limits the peak intensity of the intermediate black hole radiation to no more than 10% of the radiation density at Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Our findings indicate that the isotropic radiation background from intermediate black holes could potentially be detected by next-generation instruments capable of measuring the spectrum at TeV scales or by analyzing future high-precision CMB data. Additionally, we provide an estimate of the number of intermediate black holes required to generate a detectable signal. We also discuss the implications of a signal at terahertz frequencies for various theories of quantum gravity and extra dimensions

Our methodology involves identifying a weak high-frequency component within the power spectrum of stellar radial velocities, which stems from the Earth's upward acceleration due to its circular orbit around the Sun. However, the RAM model's capacity for efficient simulation of other computational models can create misleading impressions about the practical applicability of theoretical results. To address this, a formal computation model capable of efficiently simulating other computations is required. This paper introduces such a model, the Ticker Computer (TC), and demonstrates its utility. Our primary contribution involves employing the TC to encode polynomial order relations, thereby resolving an open problem and establishing a more robust foundation for 3-dimensional point set complexity theory. Specifically, we prove that $D_4(n) = \Theta(n \log^{2} n)$, where $D_4(n)$ denotes the maximum depth within 3-dimensional data sets, a parameter that encapsulates the complexity of various geometric algorithms operating in $\mathbb{R}^3$. This encoding relies on a new, explicit, and efficient simulation of a two-tape deterministic Turing machine (Turing) by a space-restricted Ticker Computer (restricted(TC)), achieved by mapping tape squares of Turing to balanced parentheses in restricted(TC). This mapping enables the verification of accepted words by a linear restricted(TC), which in turn facilitates the construction of the TC-based polynomial order relations. The resulting order, defined over a set of size $n$, exhibits an analysis time of $O(n^{2+\epsilon})$ and a construction time of $O(n^{3/2}\log^{k} n)$ for any $k \geq 0$. Furthermore, we detail a method to encode planar polynomial orders, which serves as a component in the broader encoding scheme. This encoding achieves an analysis complexity of $O(n^{1.63})$, improving upon the previous best bound of $O(n^{1.68})$. These orders are particularly pertinent to the study of planar (and by extension, spatial) data structures. By combining this new TC-based encoding with a previously developed weaker variant, we derive a novel lower bound for $D_4(n)$, the linear depth problem in 3D. This bound implies that no algorithm can solve the problem with a time complexity better than $O(D_4(n)^{5/3})$. Consequently, we establish the previously open result that $D_4(n) = \Omega(n \log^{2} n)$, where the constant factor is $1/(8\sqrt{2})$. the automorphism group $\text{Aut}(X)$ acts transitively on $X$. We define the transitivity degree of $X$ as the maximal integer $m$ for which the $\text{Aut}(X)$-action on $X$ is $m$-transitive; if the action is $m$-transitive for every $m$, the degree is infinite. In this work, we calculate the transitivity degree for all quasi-affine toric varieties and numerous homogeneous spaces of algebraic groups, while also examining a conjecture and several open questions concerning this invariant.

Transitivity degrees for quasi-affine toric varieties $(\mathbb{C}^n,S)$ are derived using the depth of the face semigroup $S$. Specifically, a pair $(\mathbb{C}^n,S)$ is $k$-transitive if and only if $S$ has depth at least $k+1$. For homogeneous spaces $G/H$, the situation is more complex, though we conjecture that the transitivity degree is deeply linked to the rank of a specific subgroup of the Weyl group of $G$ that stabilizes a coset of $H$.

We introduce the concept of $k$-homogeneity for algebraic varieties, denoting the maximal such $k$ (or infinity if all higher levels apply) as the $k$-homogeneity rank of $X$, written $\text{hkr}(X)$. This rank equals the transitivity degree of $X$ whenever $X$ is quasi-homogeneous. Determining $\text{hkr}(X)$ for classical homogeneous spaces remains challenging. However, we have established upper bounds based on Dynkin diagrams and specific lower bounds. Additionally, we propose a method to construct varieties with arbitrarily high transitivity degrees or $k$-homogeneity ranks.

Our approach to finding lower bounds for $\text{hkr}(G/B)$ leverages Lusztig's work on canonical bases and the Weyl group, combined with Brion's characterization of the toric variety $\text{Orb}(G/B,1)$. To address lower bounds for other homogeneous spaces, we developed a computational algorithm to determine the transitivity degree of any given quasi-homogeneous variety $(G/H,\bar{H})$. Our findings indicate that $\text{hkr}(G/H)$ is frequently determined by the structure of parabolic subgroups within $G$ containing $H$.

A key feature of these systems is their finite set of solutions, which can be effectively represented using the RootSummary data structure. RootSummary separates the parameterized nature of polynomial systems into two distinct components: (i) the primary solutions, which depend on a finite number of parameters, and (ii) the multiplicity of each primary solution. Existing methods typically generate RootSummaries directly from Gröbner bases or parametric Gröbner bases. However, these approaches often struggle to accurately compute multiplicity or fail to identify all primary solutions when multiplicity is high. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel algorithm that represents RootSummaries as parametric cells. Each cell is defined by specific parameter regions and indices, describing how the resolved multiplicity and primary solutions change as parameters vary. Our method calculates these properties by evaluating RootSummaries at generic parameter values. We demonstrate that these parametric cells can be efficiently constructed using local information, such as the characteristic matrices of resolved solutions derived from Gröbner basis computations. Furthermore, we show that this framework enables the efficient generation of other important outputs in parametric elimination theory, including equidimensional components, the support of the scheme, and the generic Hilbert-Samuel function. Numerical validation is provided through a collection of polynomial systems from both theoretical research and practical applications. Additionally, an open-source software package implementing this approach is available at \url{https://github.com/RootSummary}. Question-Answer pairs serve as a valuable resource for training extraction models to identify coreferent entities within a specific domain. However, most existing datasets rely on free-text descriptions to define coreference groups, a format that is difficult for machines to process. This limitation hinders the training of models capable of directly consuming stream data to produce output suitable for downstream tasks. To address this, we introduce QuaQA, a dataset comprising 12,000 questions paired with associated answers and coreference annotations extracted from SQuAD and TriviaQA. These answers function as explicit, machine-readable coreference annotations that can guide the training of coreference resolution models. We propose a straightforward method for learning to resolve coreference using these pairs, achieving state-of-the-art results in weather domain-specific entity resolution with an F1 score of 0.772. Additionally, we demonstrate that the learned representations enhance the performance of various tasks within the weather domain, including weather data quality filtering and precipitation nowcasting. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/roberts92/QuaQA.

While numerous local minimization techniques exist, globally convergent methods—such as simulated annealing, evolution strategies, and particle swarm optimization—are computationally expensive and often struggle to accurately and efficiently identify the minimum for complex, high-dimensional costs. This work introduces a novel algorithm that determines the exact minimum of a differentiable function and its Hessian by locally averaging locally minimal gradient vector fields derived from various evolution strategies. Although Quantum Mechanics (Q.M.) effectively models atomic and subatomic entities, its application to larger biological structures like cancer cells remains uncommon. This work introduces a novel mathematical framework within Q.M. capable of estimating the survival duration and cell division cycles for macroscopic objects. The paper demonstrates this method by calculating the lifespans and division cycles for a cancer cell, a bacterium, and a human. Furthermore, this approach offers a new perspective for examining biological systems at the cellular division level. This method represents an advancement over the $\lambda$ decay model, which is frequently used in cancer research. By determining the potential lifespan of a cancer cell, clinicians can establish the optimal timing for chemotherapy. Additionally, this technique may assist in identifying the cancer cell's origin based on its cell type. The proposed formula demonstrates greater precision compared to $\lambda$ decay models applied to radioactive decay and chemical reaction kinetics. This research paves the way for the first application of quantum biological mathematics in predicting cancer cell survival. Consequently, this could lead to refined clinical guidelines regarding chemotherapy administration. Finally, the findings are published under an Open Access model.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) has seen recent progress in utilizing natural language to represent states. However, the most common method involves applying off-the-shelf Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools to encode language states, an approach that is uncontrolled and yields opaque, difficult-to-interpret representations. This paper introduces an alternative method for encoding natural language states by explicitly modeling them as logical formulas over a lexicon and a set of world variables. This proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, it enables post-hoc interpretability by mapping network activations to logical components, revealing that learned representations capture relevant world variables and that neural network layers function as compositional hierarchies.

These applications demand that RSUs be rapidly and efficiently deployed. This paper introduces a general, data-driven framework for selecting optimal RSU locations using road network data from map applications. The method leverages road network information to establish new RSUs at positions that maximize coverage. The results indicate that the proposed approach can locate RSUs in areas previously uncovered by the existing infrastructure. Furthermore, a comparative analysis demonstrates that this method is both more efficient and of higher quality than current state-of-the-art techniques. This study examines both instantaneous and averaged digital transmission metrics within a simplified channel model to derive their statistical distributions. Our findings show that the average metric is significantly less sensitive to instantaneous metric fluctuations caused by transmission impairments, producing lower variance and a simpler computation process. This metric can be effectively employed in various digital transmission monitoring applications. For example, in coexistence scenarios, a metric with lower sensitivity to instantaneous fluctuations is preferable to prevent digital transmission monitoring from interfering with the signal under observation. Conversely, in cases where monitoring interference is unacceptable, such as in optical metro applications, more advanced monitoring solutions may be required. This research also explores how parameters like window size influence the statistical properties of the average metric. Coexistence refers to the scenario where multiple optical signals are transmitted over a shared physical medium. In this context, it is essential to avoid monitoring-induced impairments that could degrade one or more of the co-transmitted signals. Digital transmission monitoring involves periodically sampling the optical signal and comparing it against a database of known modulated symbols. Any detected discrepancies are interpreted as indicators of transmission impairments.

In neutron stars, the most significant contribution comes from p-wave annihilations occurring in magnetospheres, where neutrinos are strongly boosted by the high electron number density. For dark matter masses between approximately 1 GeV and 1 TeV, emissivity can reach up to 10^27 erg cm^-3 s^-1, exceeding the emissivity of hot neutron gas by several orders of magnitude. We examine how this effect influences the cooling of isolated neutron stars and X-ray binary systems, highlighting its potential detectability through gamma-ray observations. Annihilation heating can sustain temperatures as high as 10^9 K, causing neutrinos to dominate energy loss over photon radiation. This mechanism could explain the hypothesized population of hot, isolated neutron stars. Finally, we analyze systems where a dark star is embedded in a halo of non-self-annihilating dark matter. Annihilation occurring just outside the star generates a strong neutrino flux due to extreme density enhancement, potentially yielding a total luminosity 10^6 to 10^9 times greater than the neutrino emission from the neutron star itself. Such a mechanism might account for hypothetical ultra-luminous neutron stars. This scenario is particularly relevant for neutron stars situated in massive, compact objects that are not dark stars, such as stellar-mass black holes or neutron star mergers. We explore the implications for recent gamma-ray observations of neutron star systems and conclude that self-annihilating dark matter is unlikely to explain the observed excess X-ray emission in low-mass X-ray binaries. However, it remains a viable candidate for producing the high neutrino luminosities predicted by cooling models. Our study also considers dark matter that is not self-annihilating but instead decays directly into neutrinos. In this case, neutrino emission is particularly intense around dark stars and around dark stars embedded within dark matter halos. This mechanism could account for the high neutrino luminosities predicted for cooling pulsars and for a new class of ultra-luminous neutron stars. Such objects could be identified by future neutrino detectors with sensitivities exceeding 10^18 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Our proof relies on the equidistribution properties of highly visible subwords within the continued fraction expansion of irrational rotations, thereby extending a result by Araki from combinatorial dynamics to the ergodic setting. We also present a computer-assisted proof applicable to highly visible subwords in periodic words, which supports a conjecture regarding their asymptotic equidistribution. This finding is significant for computer-assisted ergodic theory, as it provides one of the few examples where a measure that is not uniquely ergodic exhibits ergodic properties relative to a specific dynamical system. A companion paper will demonstrate the necessity of this ergodic extension by providing a non-ergodic measure for suspension measures over irrational rotations where ergodicity still holds. Furthermore, [Heu15] introduces methods for suspensions of ergodic transformations, a topic typically addressed by suspending Veech measures, which we will examine in a subsequent publication. Additionally, [Heu15] offers insights into suspension measures for general minimal systems, specifically regarding their support structures.
